leads.title: Grandparents who help care for grandchildren keep their minds sharper, study finds
leads.summary: A study published on January 26, 2026 in the journal Psychology and Aging, by researchers at Tilburg University in the Netherlands led by Flavia Chereches, followed 2,887 grandparents aged over 50 (average age 67) from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. They took surveys and cognitive tests three times between 2016 and 2022. The researchers asked whether grandparents had cared for a grandchild in the past year, how often, and what kind of care: watching grandchildren overnight, caring for them when ill, playing with them, helping with homework, driving them to school and activities, and preparing meals. Grandparents who provided childcare scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests than those who did not, even after adjusting for age, health and other factors. This was true no matter how often they helped or what kind of care they gave. Grandmothers who provided care also showed less decline on the cognitive tests over the study period than grandmothers who did not; the study did not report a similar finding for grandfathers. The lead researcher said being a caregiving grandparent seemed to matter more for thinking skills than how often grandparents provided care. This is an observational study, so it shows a link, not proof that caregiving causes better memory. More research is needed, and caregiving that feels stressful or unsupported may differ from caregiving freely given in a supportive family.

leads.title: From Hostel Room Model to 1500+ Foldable Buildings: IIT Grads Build Infrastructure That Travels
leads.summary: This article has been published in partnership with Kalaari Capital. Five weeks after the Chennai floods, most of the volunteers had gone home. In the first few days, help had seemed to come from everywhere. People arrived with food, water and relief material. Among them was Shreeram Ravichandran, then a second-year civil engineering student at IIT Madras with Engineers Without Borders. As the weeks passed, he began noticing something the first rush of relief could not solve. In settlements between Chennai’s OMR and ECR, homes made of thatch had been washed away. Families had lost belongings and the spaces they had lived in, sometimes within hours. “Within just moments, you lose your complete home and all your belongings. Everything is gone,” he recalls. Modulus later developed modular buildings for places where conventional construction is difficult.   The floods had affected Shreeram too, but differently. His neighbourhood faced power cuts and interruptions in food supply. The building he lived in remained standing. “For these people, they just didn’t know what they were going to do the next week or the next day, where they would stay,” he says. “It had just become empty land.” Long after the water receded, that difference stayed with him. Relief could arrive within days. A permanent house could take years. What was a family supposed to do in between? The years between a tent and a home Back at IIT Madras, Shreeram and his fellow students began trying to understand that gap. They looked at what had happened after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and found that permanent rehabilitation could stretch across several years.
